reports.title: Eritrea: Selected Issues and Statistical Appendix (IMF Country Report No. 03/166)
reports.description: The most recent IMF document with substantive Eritrea CPI content locatable this round (2003; report data through 2002). Directly extracted via OCR (the PDF is a scanned image with no text layer) from Chapter V, paragraph 87: "Until recently, the authorities have used two measures of inflation, one produced by the Bank of Eritrea (BE) and the other established by the National Eritrea Statistics and Evaluation Office (SEO)... The SEO began compiling its own measure of the CPI in January 1996." Table V.1 sources line: "Sources: Bank of Eritrea; Eritrea Statistical and Evaluation Office; Ethiopian authorities; and IMF staff estimates." PAST TENSE and flagged accordingly: this describes 1994-2002 practice with no confirmation it continues. No live NSEO (National Statistics and Evaluation Office) website was found — only third-party aggregator profile pages (knoema.com, ghdx.healthdata.org). A 2019 IMF Article IV mission occurred but its end-of-mission press release contains no CPI figures or agency citation, and no full Board-approved staff report after 2003 could be confirmed as published — Eritrea has a documented history of delayed/absent Article IV consultations.
reports.cadence_note: One-off country report; no evidence of a current recurring Eritrean CPI publication was found this round.

reports.title: Constitution of Eritrea (1997)
reports.description: Eritrea's 1997 Constitution, ratified but never fully implemented/promulgated into force. Article 1(5): "Eritrea is a unitary State divided into units of local government. The powers and duties of these units shall be determined by law." Verified directly via PDF text extraction. No implementing body or fiscal mechanism is named — the constitutional mandate is general and, per er-un-coi-proclamation-86-1996, was never given fiscal substance at the regional (zoba) level.

reports.title: UN Commission of Inquiry on Human Rights in Eritrea — Chapter V (quoting Proclamation No. 86/1996)
reports.publisher: UN Human Rights Council Commission of Inquiry on Eritrea
reports.description: A UN Commission of Inquiry report (A/HRC/29/CRP.1) that quotes Eritrea's own Proclamation No. 86/1996 verbatim with paragraph/article numbers; the proclamation itself is not independently available online in full text, so this UN document is the best available evidence. Directly verified via PDF text extraction. Paragraph 260: "In April 1996, Proclamation No. 86/1996 was adopted. It abolished the historical nine provinces of Eritrea and established six administrative regions or zobas... Southern Red Sea; Northern Red Sea; Anseba; Gash-Barka; Southern; and Central." Paragraph 263: "Article 13(1) of the Proclamation states that baito zobas are to prepare regional development programmes... Regional assemblies do not have fiscal authority but are mandated to collect local revenues." This last clause is the key finding: Eritrea's regional (zoba) tier has NO fiscal transfer mechanism analogous to other African countries' provincial equalisation/dotation systems — a genuine structural negative finding, not a research gap.
reports.cadence_note: One-off report (2015), quoting a one-off 1996 legislative instrument.

_dropped.why: Bloc-membership status, recorded for future reference rather than as an edge attempt: IGAD's own press release (12 December 2025) states "IGAD has taken note of the decision by the Government of the State of Eritrea to withdraw from the Organisation... Since June 2023, IGAD notes with regret that Eritrea has not participated in IGAD meetings, programmes, or activities." Eritrea's regional-bloc relationships are unusually unstable (also suspended from COMESA in 2006, per conflicting secondary sources below) — any future statistical-harmonisation edge involving Eritrea and a regional bloc should be timestamped precisely.

COMESA membership status for Eritrea is genuinely unresolved from primary sources: USTR's current member list and COMESA's own country page (naming an active National COMESA Focal Point) suggest Eritrea remains a member, while Wikipedia's membership table lists a 2007 departure. No primary COMESA Council/Summit legal decision document confirming suspension or withdrawal was locatable this round — recorded as an open question, not asserted either way.
